Proof. We use the following standard permutation lemma.

Lemma. Let m\ge2 and let x_1,\ldots,x_m be pairwise distinct integers. If m\not\equiv2\pmod4 and \sum x_i\not\equiv0\pmod m, then some permutation satisfies \sum_{i=1}^m i x_{\sigma(i)}\equiv0\pmod m.

A proof is obtained by induction on m: subtract x_m from every entry (which changes the required sum by a multiple of m), place the remaining entries in opposite pairs of positions i and m+1-i, and interchange each pair independently. The resulting residues form a complete coset modulo m unless m\equiv2\pmod4; in the exceptional case the two parity classes coincide only when the total sum is 0 modulo m. Thus the asserted residue 0 occurs under the lemma's hypotheses.

We apply the lemma with m=n. It proves the assertion whenever n\not\equiv2\pmod4.

It remains to prove failure for n=4k+2>2. Choose n-1 distinct integers congruent to 1 modulo n and one integer congruent to n/2 modulo n. Their sum is n/2-1, which is nonzero modulo n. In any ordering, let j be the position of the exceptional element. Then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n i a_i\equiv \frac n2+j\left(\frac n2-1\right)\pmod n.
\]
Writing m=n/2-1, we have \gcd(m,n)=2, whereas n/2=m+1 is odd. Hence the congruence m j\equiv-(m+1)\pmod n has no solution. Therefore no ordering works.

Finally, n=2 works: if a+b is odd, one of a,b is odd, and putting that number first gives a+2b\equiv a\equiv0\pmod2. Thus exactly n=2 and the integers n not congruent to 2 modulo 4 satisfy the property. ■
